title: Théorie des cycles algébriques : conjectures de Hodge, Tate, Lefschetz, Weil : notes manuscrites (s.d.), lettre (1965).

deep.reconstruction:
This page continues the previous one, which went through examples case by case. The setup seems to be the following: X is smooth projective, Y is a (generic) hyperplane section, and π is the monodromy group of the family of sections (Lefschetz pencil). For each codimension i the notes use three groups:
- A^i, the Chow group of codimension-i cycles;
- J^i, its algebraically trivial part (intermediate-Jacobian type);
- N^i, the Néron–Severi quotient A^i/J^i.
The sign ≡ seems to mean 'is determined by Y / comes from Y, up to finite groups (and up to p-torsion in characteristic p)'.

Reading the indices consistently, N appears to be dim X + 1 (N may be the dimension of an ambient space). Check against the examples:
- 'N=3': X is a surface and Y a curve. The vanishing-cycle problem concerns J^1(X)=Pic^0(X) inside J^1(Y)=Jac(Y), and the Hodge index theorem for surfaces appears.
- 'N=4' (this page): X is a threefold and Y a surface. The 'essential groups' are J^2(X) and N^1(X). J^2(X) is the intermediate Jacobian, governed by H^3, the middle cohomology. The 'essential homomorphism' is N^1(X) → N^1(Y), i.e. NS(X) → NS(Y), which is injective by Lefschetz.

Grothendieck then poses a problem: define an intrinsic complement of NS(X) inside NS(Y), made of algebraic vanishing cycles, and give a precise meaning to N^1(X) ≃ N^1(Y)^π (invariants under monodromy). This is the algebraic-cycle analogue of the invariant-cycle theorem and the vanishing-cycle decomposition: H^{n-1}(Y) = image of H^{n-1}(X) ⊕ the vanishing part E, orthogonal for cup product, with E^π = 0.

Below the rule he extracts the general pattern, consistent with 'N = dim X + 1'.
- N = 2m+1, so dim X = 2m: A^i(X) ≡ 0 for i ≥ m+1. In cohomology the Gysin map H^{j-2}(Y) → H^j(X) is surjective for j > dim X, i.e. 2i > 2m.
- N = 2m, so dim X = 2m-1 is odd: N^m(X) ≡ 0, because H^{2m} lies above the middle degree. Hence J^m(X) ≡ A^m(X): only the intermediate-Jacobian part, governed by the middle H^{2m-1}, is essential. Also A^i ≡ 0 for i ≥ m+1.

In short, this is a programme for Lefschetz-type theorems on Chow groups. Low-dimensional cycles (dimension below dim X/2) should be 'carried by' the hyperplane section. The only new ('essential') information of X sits in the middle: the intermediate Jacobian and the NS groups of codimension just below the middle. Their relation to Y should be governed by monodromy invariants plus a vanishing-cycle complement.
errors: The isomorphism N^1(X) ≃ N^1(Y)^π can only hold after tensoring with Q (or up to finite index and torsion, and up to p-torsion in characteristic p). It makes sense only for the geometric generic hyperplane section (or a very general one), not for an arbitrary Y. For a pencil, X must be replaced by its blow-up along the base locus, which adds classes.

The statements 'A^i(X) ≡ 0 for i ≥ m+1' are conjectural Chow-theoretic Lefschetz statements, not theorems. Modulo rational equivalence they are open in general: they follow from Bloch–Beilinson type conjectures. The notation ≡ (meaning roughly 'comes from Y up to finite groups') is never defined on the page.
Identifying N with dim X + 1 is my inference from the index pattern; the page does not say it explicitly.

ideas.what: Lefschetz-type principle for Chow groups: cycles of dimension below dim X/2 are supported on (come from) a hyperplane section Y; only the 'middle' groups of X are essential.
ideas.modern_name: Conjectural Lefschetz/Gysin surjectivity for Chow groups (Hartshorne's question; consequences of Bloch–Beilinson; Nori connectivity)
ideas.where_published: Related cohomological Lefschetz statements are in SGA 2 and 'Standard conjectures on algebraic cycles' (1969); the Chow-group version is not known to me in Grothendieck's published texts.

ideas.what: An intrinsic complement of NS(X) inside NS(Y) (algebraic vanishing cycles), and the meaning of NS(X) ≃ NS(Y)^π.
ideas.modern_name: Algebraic part of the vanishing-cycle decomposition; global invariant cycle theorem applied to Néron–Severi; orthogonal complement for the intersection form (Hodge index); Noether–Lefschetz phenomena
ideas.usually_credited_to: Deligne (Weil II, SGA 7 vanishing-cycle formalism); Lefschetz; Noether–Lefschetz theory
ideas.where_published: SGA 7 (Deligne/Katz chapters) for vanishing cycles; the NS version as such is unsure.

ideas.what: Case split by parity: odd dim X gives essential groups J^m (intermediate Jacobian) with N^m ≡ 0; even dim X gives essential middle groups with A^{>m} ≡ 0.
ideas.modern_name: Coniveau/weight bookkeeping matching the weak Lefschetz theorem

missed.claim: Grothendieck formulates, as an open problem, a functorial 'vanishing-cycle complement' at the level of Néron–Severi groups (and, on the previous page, of Jacobians). The aim is an intrinsic splitting N^1(Y) = N^1(X) ⊕ (algebraic vanishing cycles) compatible with monodromy, set inside a systematic programme of Lefschetz theorems for Chow groups. The ideas are now standard, rationally via Hodge index or the standard conjectures, and as conjectures via Bloch–Beilinson. This particular early formulation (c. 1965–71) of Chow-level Lefschetz expectations is only marginally of historical interest.
missed.quote: Pb définir un complémentaire intrinsèque de N^1(X) dans N^1(Y) (cycles évanouissants). Donner un sens à la formule N^1(X) ≃ N^1(Y)^π
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It is an early trace of Grothendieck anticipating Hartshorne/Nori-type Lefschetz conjectures for Chow groups. That is mildly interesting historically but not new mathematics.

deep.surprise_reason: The page sketches Chow-group Lefschetz expectations and a vanishing-cycle complement for NS, all of which are now standard or conjectured elsewhere (Bloch–Beilinson, Nori, Deligne). The only point of note is that this is an early, informal anticipation.
transcription_corrections: '[-N^1-]N^1(X)': the first symbol is a struck-through letter (an overwritten N), so the formula reads N^1(X) ≃ N^1(Y)^π.
'on[?] trouve alors': the scribble before 'trouve' could also be 'il' or 'on'; the meaning is unchanged.
The word read as 'intrinsèque' is uncertain in the image; the parallel phrase on the previous page is 'complémentaire naturel'.
